explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "Behold, I will stir up against Babylon and against the people of Leb-kamai the spirit of a destroyer." (Jeremiah 51:1) Leb-kamai is another name used here for Babylon's people. Not a famine, not a plague. A destroyer.

I get why a famine comes to mind, friend. Famine shows up in plenty of Bible warnings. But this verse says something different: the LORD will stir up "the spirit of a destroyer" against Babylon and the people of Leb-kamai. (Jeremiah 51:1) It's an army-sized word, not a pantry-sized one.

A plague on cattle is a real thing in the Bible, but it's from another story. Here the LORD says He will stir up "the spirit of a destroyer" against Babylon and the people of Leb-kamai. (Jeremiah 51:1) No cows in this verse, friend. Just the destroyer.

True, baker. The LORD says strangers will come against Babylon "from every side in her day of disaster." (Jeremiah 51:2) They come to winnow her and empty her land. Winnowing is tossing grain so the wind blows the chaff away, and I think that picture is a rough one for Babylon.

Close, but this one is true. The verse says the strangers "will come against her from every side in her day of disaster." (Jeremiah 51:2) So the timing is right there in the text. Her day of disaster is when they arrive, friend.

Yes, spare. The orders say, "Do not spare her young men; devote all her army to destruction!" (Jeremiah 51:3) It's a heavy line, friend, and I think it's okay to just let it be heavy. The LORD is speaking about Babylon's army here.

Warn is a fair guess, baker, since warnings come up a lot in the prophets. But the verse says, "Do not spare her young men." (Jeremiah 51:3) The word is spare. It's a hard line, and the text doesn't soften it.

Trust is a good word, but it isn't this one. The verse says, "Do not spare her young men; devote all her army to destruction!" (Jeremiah 51:3) The missing word is spare, friend. This is a heavy part of the passage.

I see why that sounds right, baker. Their land is full of guilt, and that's serious. But the LORD says, "Israel and Judah have not been abandoned by their God, the LORD of Hosts." (Jeremiah 51:5) The guilt is real, and so is the LORD still being their God.

False is right, friend. The LORD says Israel and Judah "have not been abandoned by their God, the LORD of Hosts, though their land is full of guilt before the Holy One of Israel." (Jeremiah 51:5) Both things are in the same verse. I read that line like a warm biscuit on a cold day. Wait, I mean cookie.

explanations.answer: It is the time of the LORD's vengeance
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The call says, "Flee from Babylon! Escape with your lives! Do not be destroyed in her punishment. For this is the time of the LORD's vengeance; He will pay her what she deserves." (Jeremiah 51:6) The reason is right there in the verse. When the text gives the reason, I just read it out loud.

explanations.answer: Her great river is about to flood
explanations.explanation: A flood would make people run, friend, I'll give you that. But the verse gives a different reason: "this is the time of the LORD's vengeance; He will pay her what she deserves." (Jeremiah 51:6) No flood is mentioned there.

explanations.answer: Her king has ordered everyone out
explanations.explanation: That would be a quick way to clear a city, baker. But this call isn't from Babylon's king. The reason given is, "this is the time of the LORD's vengeance; He will pay her what she deserves." (Jeremiah 51:6) The text never mentions a king giving the order.

Drunk, yes. "Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk." (Jeremiah 51:7) It's a picture, friend, not a recipe. The verse goes on to say the nations drank her wine, so the nations have gone mad.

Rich makes sense with a gold cup, baker, I'll give you that. But the verse says Babylon was "a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk." (Jeremiah 51:7) The cup is gold, but the earth gets drunk, not rich.

If only, friend. The verse says the opposite. Babylon was "a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk," and "the nations have gone mad." (Jeremiah 51:7) Nobody walks away wise from that cup.

explanations.answer: Wail for her and get her balm
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says, "Wail for her; get her balm for her pain; perhaps she can be healed." (Jeremiah 51:8) Balm is a soothing ointment for a wound. That line has some tenderness in it, and I think it's worth noticing.

Walls would be a natural next step, friend. But the text calls for something else: "Wail for her; get her balm for her pain." (Jeremiah 51:8) Nothing here about rebuilding. It's about mourning and treating her pain.

explanations.answer: Crown a new king over her
explanations.explanation: A new king sounds like a plan, baker, but it isn't in this verse. After she "has fallen and been shattered," the call is, "Wail for her; get her balm for her pain; perhaps she can be healed." (Jeremiah 51:8) Mourning and balm, not a coronation.

I get the hope, baker, and the verse before it kept that hope open with "perhaps." But the next verse says, "We tried to heal Babylon, but she could not be healed." (Jeremiah 51:9) They tried, and it didn't work.

False, friend. The text says, "We tried to heal Babylon, but she could not be healed." (Jeremiah 51:9) They give it a real effort, and she still can't be healed. That's why the next words are, "Abandon her!"

explanations.answer: What the LORD our God has accomplished
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The call says, "The LORD has brought forth our vindication; come, let us tell in Zion what the LORD our God has accomplished." (Jeremiah 51:10) Zion is Jerusalem. The telling is about what the LORD did, and it's good news to share.

explanations.answer: How great Babylon used to be
explanations.explanation: That's a nostalgic idea, friend, but it isn't what the verse says. The call is, "come, let us tell in Zion what the LORD our God has accomplished." (Jeremiah 51:10) The story to tell is about the LORD's work, not Babylon's good old days.

A getaway report would be juicy, baker, but the verse doesn't have one. It says, "come, let us tell in Zion what the LORD our God has accomplished." (Jeremiah 51:10) The telling is about what the LORD did, and it happens in Zion.

explanations.answer: His plan is to destroy Babylon
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. "The LORD has aroused the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because His plan is aimed at Babylon to destroy her." (Jeremiah 51:11) The Medes were a people from the east, and the LORD stirs their kings for this plan. The reason is stated right in the verse.

explanations.answer: His plan is to punish Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt shows up in a lot of Bible stories, friend, but not here. The verse says, "His plan is aimed at Babylon to destroy her." (Jeremiah 51:11) The Medes are stirred up for Babylon.

explanations.answer: His plan is to test the Medes
explanations.explanation: Testing is a Bible word, baker, but this verse doesn't use it for the Medes. It says the LORD aroused their kings "because His plan is aimed at Babylon to destroy her." (Jeremiah 51:11) The Medes are part of the plan, not the target of it.

True, baker. "The LORD has both devised and accomplished what He spoke against the people of Babylon." (Jeremiah 51:12) Planned and carried out, both in one verse. When He speaks, I think it's wise to listen, and I speak as someone who once ignored a timer and burned a whole batch.

This one is true, friend. The verse says, "the LORD has both devised and accomplished what He spoke against the people of Babylon." (Jeremiah 51:12) Devised means planned, and accomplished means carried out. Both are right there.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "You who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut." (Jeremiah 51:13) Waterfront and wealthy, and still her end comes. A hard line, and the text just says it plainly.

Rescue would be a nice turn, friend, but it's not what the verse says. It says, "your end has come; the thread of your life is cut." (Jeremiah 51:13) For a city rich in treasures, that's a sobering word.
A new king isn't in this verse, baker. What comes for her is, "your end has come; the thread of your life is cut." (Jeremiah 51:13) Her riches and her many waters don't change that.

Shout is right, friend. The LORD of Hosts says, "Surely I will fill you up with men as with locusts, and they will shout in triumph over you." (Jeremiah 51:14) And He swore it by Himself. That's as solid as a promise gets.

Weeping fits a lot of moments, baker, but not this one. The verse says the men "will shout in triumph over you." (Jeremiah 51:14) It's the sound of a victory shout, and the LORD of Hosts swore it by Himself.

Prayer is always a good word, friend, but it's not what the verse says. The men filling Babylon "will shout in triumph over you." (Jeremiah 51:14) A locust swarm and a victory shout, that's the picture.

Breath, yes. The verse says the goldsmith's "molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them." (Jeremiah 51:17) A goldsmith works metal, and the idol still has no life in it. Meanwhile the LORD is the One who "brings forth the wind from His storehouses." (Jeremiah 51:16)

Gold is a good guess, baker, since goldsmiths are in the verse. But it says, "his molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them." (Jeremiah 51:17) They may have plenty of gold. What they don't have is breath.

Paint would be a funny thing to be missing, friend. But the verse says, "his molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them." (Jeremiah 51:17) Molten means melted metal poured into a shape, so no paint needed. It's breath they lack.
That's right, baker. "They are worthless, a work to be mocked. In the time of their punishment they will perish." (Jeremiah 51:18) Idols can't save anybody, and here they can't even save themselves.

explanations.answer: They will be carried off as plunder
explanations.explanation: Carried off sounds like what happens to treasure, friend, but the verse says something else. "In the time of their punishment they will perish." (Jeremiah 51:18) No hauling away is mentioned, just perishing.

explanations.answer: They will be melted into new ones
explanations.explanation: Melted is a smart guess, baker, since the idols are molten images. But the verse says, "In the time of their punishment they will perish." (Jeremiah 51:18) There's no remaking in it. Perishing is the end of it.

Shatters, yes. The LORD says, "You are My war club, My weapon for battle. With you I shatter nations; with you I bring kingdoms to ruin." (Jeremiah 51:20) The text doesn't name who the war club is, so I won't guess, friend. It just says what the LORD does with it.

Guarding is a good job, baker, but a war club isn't for that here. The LORD says, "With you I shatter nations; with you I bring kingdoms to ruin." (Jeremiah 51:20) Shatter is the word, and it comes up again and again in the verses after.

Gathering is a gentle word, friend, and this verse isn't gentle. The LORD says, "With you I shatter nations; with you I bring kingdoms to ruin." (Jeremiah 51:20) A war club shatters. It doesn't gather.

explanations.answer: All the evil they did in Zion
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, "Before your very eyes I will repay Babylon and all the dwellers of Chaldea for all the evil they have done in Zion." (Jeremiah 51:24) Zion is Jerusalem. The reason is stated right there.

explanations.answer: All the gold they took from Egypt
explanations.explanation: Gold is a fun guess, friend, but Egypt isn't in this verse. The LORD says He will repay Babylon and the dwellers of Chaldea "for all the evil they have done in Zion." (Jeremiah 51:24) The text names the evil, and it's in Zion.

explanations.answer: All the towers they built too high
explanations.explanation: That sounds like another famous Babylon story, baker, but it isn't what this verse says. The LORD will repay them "for all the evil they have done in Zion." (Jeremiah 51:24) Zion is Jerusalem, and the reason is the evil done there.

I see why you might think so, baker. Stones from old buildings get reused all the time. But the LORD says, "No one shall retrieve from you a cornerstone or a foundation stone, because you will become desolate forever." (Jeremiah 51:26) Nothing gets pulled out to build with again.

False is right, friend. The LORD says, "No one shall retrieve from you a cornerstone or a foundation stone, because you will become desolate forever." (Jeremiah 51:26) Not even the stones that hold a building up get taken. That's how complete it is.
